title: “The Jig Is Up”: Voters Resoundingly Reject Republicans Who Wanted to Run Elections
author: Alex Burness
content:
The most closely-watched elections office in the country flipped blue on
Tuesday as Georgia, where Donald Trump famously pressured Republican Secretary
of State Brad Raffensperger to [“find” thousands of non-existent
votes](https://www.washingtonpost.com/politics/trump-raffensperger-call-
georgia-vote/2021/01/03/d45acb92-4dc4-11eb-bda4-615aaefd0555_story.html) to
overturn his 2020 defeat, overwhelmingly elected Democrat Penny Reynolds Brown
to succeed Raffensperger.

She is the first Black woman to be elected secretary of state in Georgia, and
will be the first Democrat to hold the job in 20 years. Her top priority, she
told _Bolts_ , is to make voting easier for people struggling to contend with
the Georgia GOP’s [restrictions](https://boltsmag.org/georgia-runoff-election-
early-voting/) on early voting, voter ID, and ballot dropboxes.

“It’s not in the Republican Party’s best interest that every eligible Georgian
vote,” said Reynolds Brown, a former Fulton County (Atlanta) judge who won by
12 percentage points on Tuesday. She defeated Republican Tim Fleming, who has
baselessly alleged that mail voting produces fraud, and backed voting
restrictions as a state lawmaker.

“If you don’t have the policies that the people will vote for, then you try to
do everything you can to eliminate the people from voting,” Reynolds Brown
said.

Democrats seeking oversight of elections accomplished [much more than the
Georgia flip](https://boltsmag.org/whats-on-the-ballot/guide-to-2026-general-
election/) on Tuesday. Out of the states that elected a secretary of state
this fall, Democrats swept the swing states, and then some. They won all blue
states, plus every state that Trump had won by up to 12 percentage points just
two years ago.

They also secured the power to choose who runs elections in many other
states—such as Texas, or Pennsylvania—where the secretary of state is
appointed.

Out of all 17 states with the tightest 2024 presidential margins, the only one
where the GOP is on track to control election administration moving forward is
North Carolina—and that’s only because of a [Republican power-
grab](https://boltsmag.org/north-carolina-republicans-upend-election-
administration/) in late 2024 to seize control from the Democratic governor.

This election saw Democrats flip secretary of state offices in Indiana and
Ohio, in addition to Georgia. They held onto those offices in Arizona,
Michigan, and Nevada. In each of these states, the victorious candidates
defeated Republican competitors who at minimum support voting restrictions,
and who in some
places—[Arizona](https://www.washingtonpost.com/politics/2026/10/11/arizona-
gop-nominee-elections-chief-alexander-kolodin-built-his-career-trumps-big-
lie/) and [Nevada](https://apnews.com/article/nevada-secretary-of-state-
election-conspiracies-marchant-988849972274838c21ca3fbbd73bdd90), in
particular—are vocal election deniers.

Democrats also seized the state legislature in New Hampshire, where lawmakers
select the secretary of state, though it [remains
unclear](https://www.nhpr.org/nh-news/2026-11-05/newhampshire-nh-secretary-of-
state-legislature-scanlan) whether they will oust current Secretary David
Scanlan, a Republican. They won a legislative trifecta in Wisconsin, where
lawmakers and the governor appoint the members of a state election commission.

In Texas, Democratic Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa will inherit the power to
appoint a secretary of state.

Democrats may yet flip the elections office in Alaska, too, depending on the
outcome of the still-uncalled governor’s race; the lieutenant governor on the
winning ticket in that state will oversee elections and appoint an elections
director.

Republicans, meanwhile, flipped zero state elections offices, and had to fight
just to hold onto some of their own territory. Florida’s governor gets to
appoint the secretary of state, and Democrats lost the race for that seat by
just 1 point. In Kansas, where Donald Trump won the 2024 election by 16
points, Republican Pat Proctor has a
[lead](https://www.nytimes.com/interactive/2026/11/03/us/elections/results-
kansas-secretary-of-state.html) of roughly 9,000 votes as of Friday morning;
the Associated Press has yet to call the election.

“I’ve been calling it a reckoning,” Ohio Secretary of State-elect Allison
Russo, a Democrat who won by 3.5 percentage points on Tuesday, told _Bolts_
following the election. She’ll replace Republican Frank LaRose, [who won his
2022](https://boltsmag.org/ohio-secretary-of-state/) contest by 20 points, and
who has been a loyal soldier for years in [Trump’s attacks on
democracy](https://boltsmag.org/ohio-ends-grace-periods-for-mail-ballots/),
including by investigating unfounded claims of non-citizen voter fraud and
supporting the Department of Justice’s hunt for state-level voter data.

![](https://boltsmag.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/11/25156469753137-2400x1600.jpg)Allison Russo, the
Democrat who just won the election for Ohio secretary of state, is pictured
here in November of 2021, when she was running for Congress. (AP Photo/Jay
LaPrete, File)

“The jig is up for a lot of fear tactics,” Russo said. “This whole narrative
that we have massive non-citizen voting and fraud and it's impacting our
election results, and denying that the president lost the 2020 election—I
think most people look at this and are sick and tired of it.”

Beau Bayh, the Secretary of State-elect in Indiana, who will be the first
Democrat to hold the office in three decades, added in a call with _Bolts_ on
Thursday, “Americans, and certainly Hoosiers, have an inherent sense of right
and wrong. They’ve clearly grown tired of politicians who want to reject
election results when they don’t like them.”

Secretaries of state generally [cannot unilaterally command major
changes](https://boltsmag.org/whats-on-the-ballot/local-election-
administration/) to election law and procedure, since those powers largely
rest with state legislatures. This means, for instance, that Russo cannot undo
Ohio’s voter ID law, which she opposes and is [among the strictest in the
country](https://www.ncsl.org/elections-and-campaigns/voter-id), and that
Reynolds Brown cannot order Georgia to expand its window of early voting.

But Tuesday’s elections should make state-level elections reform much more
feasible for these two and for other officials seeking to make voting easier,
thanks to massive statehouse gains for Democrats.

Notably, for the first time in 60 years, Democrats will have [trifecta control
of Arizona](https://azmirror.com/2026/11/03/the-trifecta-democrats-declare-
victory-in-fight-for-control-of-arizona-legislature/). They’ll have [a
trifecta in
Pennsylvania](https://www.spotlightpa.org/news/2026/11/pennsylvania-house-
election-results-legislature-control-elections/) for the first time in 33
years, [and in Wisconsin](https://wisconsinexaminer.com/2026/11/04/democrats-
win-control-of-wisconsin-legislature-cementing-first-democratic-trifecta-
in-16-years/), for the first time in 16 years. Anticipating these outcomes,
voting rights advocates have been plotting various election reforms, and each
of these states is very likely to consider at least some fresh legislation in
this area next year. Supportive testimony from aligned secretaries of state
can aid in passing such reforms.

![](https://boltsmag.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/11/26299674632678-2400x1600.jpg)Garlin Gilchrist, who
currently serves as Michigan's lieutenant governor and was just elected
secretary of state, speaks during a campaign event in Detroit on Oct. 24,
2026. (AP Photo/Paul Sancya)

Democrats also appear to have made gains in the Alaska statehouse, where both
chambers are governed by unusual bipartisan coalitions. Lawmakers there are
already plotting voting reforms; Democratic State Representative Andrew Gray
told _Bolts_ on Thursday that he expects an elections bill next session that
would, among other things, create a process for Alaska voters to resolve
errors on mail ballots, such as a missing signature on a ballot sleeve, to
avoid having those ballots tossed. No such process currently exists in that
state.

Gray also said that he plans to introduce a constitutional amendment next
session to grant voting rights to non-citizen U.S. nationals from American
Samoa, many thousands of whom live in Alaska [with no voting
rights](https://boltsmag.org/prosecuted-for-voting-american-samoans-alaska/).
Democratic gains in the statehouse could boost that proposal.

Reynolds Brown said she hopes Georgia, where Democrats flipped the state House
and nearly flipped the state Senate, can unwind some of the GOP elections
policies enacted of late. Republicans in that state have, since 2020, passed a
slew of voting restrictions—stricter voter ID laws, limits on ballot
dropboxes, tighter deadlines for people requesting to vote by mail, and
more—that Reynolds Brown pledges to combat. She said she will lobby for a
fresh voting rights bill that includes expanded early voting.

But she also emphasized that she intends to use the softer powers of her
office to help people vote. In that respect, secretaries of state, who have
large staffs and budgets, can make a huge difference. For instance, in
Colorado, Democratic Secretary of State-elect Amanda Gonzalez told _Bolts_ she
intends to increase the office’s outreach to [incarcerated
voters](https://boltsmag.org/jail-voting-soars-in-colorado/), who throughout
the country are generally ignored by elections officials when they’re not
[outright blocked](https://boltsmag.org/virginia-passes-amendment-3-ending-
harsh-felony-disenfranchisement/) from voting.

![](https://boltsmag.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/11/884930172_1047468284978542_9053690928140252960_n-e1793984810224.jpeg)Indiana
Secretary of State-elect Beau Bayh speaking to students at DePauw University
on Oct. 31, during the campaign. (Facebook/Beau Bayh)

In Indiana, Bayh told _Bolts_ he will use his office’s soft powers to address
the fact that Indiana consistently has some of the country’s
[lowest](https://www.incontext.indiana.edu/2025/may-jun/article2.asp) turnout
rates. That initiative, he said, will include allocating staff to college
campuses, where student voters have faced barriers thanks to [GOP-backed voter
ID rules](https://boltsmag.org/indiana-banning-student-id-for-voting/).

Bayh also said he’d dispatch staff to polling places to confirm that disabled
voters are accommodated; he said he was disturbed to hear on the campaign
trail from disabled people who struggled to vote.

In Ohio, Russo spoke of older voters who she has seen struggling to satisfy
the state’s strict voter ID rules.

“We want to make sure that every eligible Ohioan, no matter where they live or
what their circumstances are, has convenient access to their right to
vote—period,” Russo said. “When we have people who are eligible to vote, we
should be doing everything we can to make sure that they can carry out their
right to vote, and not create additional barriers.”
